title: Examples of RCTs in public programmes
section: Yemen: testing whether internships help youth find work
text:
Yemen: testing whether internships help youth find work

Sanaa and Aden, YemenStratified RCT583 young graduates2013–2015



The problem
Young jobseekers in Yemen often face a catch-22: firms are reluctant to hire someone without prior work experience, yet that experience is hard to gain without first being hired. Early jobs matter because they build both job-specific and soft skills, but firms may under-invest in providing them - a reluctance that can be sharper still in a fragile, conflict-affected setting. Job opportunities for young graduates were also increasingly scarce following Yemen’s 2011–12 political crisis.


What was done
The Enterprise Revitalization and Employment Pilot (EREP) tested a subsidised-internship model: the programme paid half the cost of a six-month internship, with the host firm covering the rest, and matched applicants to firms based on the firm’s stated requirements. Recent graduates in Sanaa and Aden applied online and were screened for eligibility before being considered.



What experimentation sought to answer

“Can a subsidised matchmaking programme help young jobseekers gain their first work experience, and does that experience translate into better employment outcomes afterwards?”



The programme

  The programmeEnterprise Revitalization and Employment Pilot (EREP), internship component: matching grants covering half the cost of a six-month internship, plus matchmaking between graduates and firms
  WhereRepublic of Yemen; Sanaa and Aden
  Who is randomised583 eligible youth (Yemeni, Sanaa/Aden residents, graduated within 2 years), to treatment (430) or control (153)
  The designStratified RCT: treatment group offered matchmaking to internships subsidised at 50% of cost, for up to six months
  Outcomes trackedEmployment, months worked and earnings, via a follow-up phone survey
  Starting point3,487 eligible youth applied; 500 were randomly invited to a two-day basic skills training (477 attended)



Key steps and dates

  ApplicationsOct–Dec 2013
  →
  Skills-training invitationJan 2014; training Feb–Mar 2014
  →
  Random assignment
  →
  MatchmakingMar–May 2014
  →
  Follow-up surveyMar 2015



How the programme was tested
The programme launched in August 2013 through a project website, media events and campus outreach. Applications ran from October to December 2013, closing with 3,487 eligible applicants. Of these, 500 were randomly invited to a two-day basic skills training - chosen with probability proportional to the demand for their specialisation - and 477 attended.
The resulting experimental sample of 583 individuals was randomly assigned, within strata defined by specialisation and city, to a treatment group of 430 (offered matchmaking to a subsidised internship) or a control group of 153. Eleven human resource advisors then matched treatment-group applicants to firms based on the firm’s requirements, sending CVs for firms to interview and decide whether to offer a placement.


  
  3,487
  eligible applicants

  

  
  500 invited to training
  477 attended

  

  
  583 experimental sample
  assigned within 39 strata

  
  
  

  
  430 treatment
  offered matchmaking

  
  153 control
  no internship match

Note: Applicants were randomly invited to basic skills training, then the resulting sample was randomly assigned, within specialisation-and-city strata, to a treatment group offered internship matchmaking or a control group.


Why this design. Strength: randomising within strata defined by specialisation and city, among applicants who had already been invited to training, helps ensure the treatment and control groups started out comparable in skills and local job-market conditions. Limitation: more applicants were assigned to treatment than there were internship placements available, so actual take-up (36.7%) fell well below the treatment assignment rate - which is why the study reports both an intention-to-treat effect and a larger effect scaled up for those who actually took up an internship.



What the programme achieved


+17 pp / +42 pp
More likely to have worked at all in 2014
Being offered internship matchmaking raised the chance of having worked at all during 2014 by 17 percentage points on an intention-to-treat basis, from a 61% employment rate in the control group, and by 42 percentage points among those who actually took up an internship.


+0.35 s.d. / +0.85 s.d.
Employment gains persisted months after the internship ended
On a standardised index of employment outcomes measured three to five months after internships ended, effects remained statistically significant: 0.35 standard deviations on an intention-to-treat basis, and 0.85 standard deviations for those who took up an internship.


36.7%
Take-up among those assigned to treatment
Only 158 of the 430 people assigned to treatment were actually matched to and completed an internship placement, reflecting how binding capacity constraints were relative to demand for internship positions.



The internship raised employment more for male applicants than for female applicants, so the programme did not close the pre-existing gender gap in employment outcomes. Because the evaluation covers only one year of the programme rather than the two originally planned, the study had limited statistical power to say precisely how much smaller the effect was for women.


Conflict escalated partway through the programme: Houthi forces took control of Sanaa in September 2014, and the second year of the pilot was cancelled, roughly halving the intended sample and reducing statistical power. The follow-up survey was also fielded earlier and more narrowly than planned, amid displacement and shortages of fuel, electricity and water. It also remains possible that some of the employment gains for treated youth came partly at the expense of other jobseekers in the economy - a general equilibrium effect this study could not measure.


  Further reading
  
  McKenzie, D., Assaf, N., and Cusolito, A. P. 2016. The demand for, and impact of, youth internships: Evidence from a randomized experiment in Yemen. IZA Journal of Labor & Development, 5(1), 1–15.

title: Informed consent in RCT data collection
text:
This page explains what informed consent means in the context of a European Union (EU) randomised controlled trial (RCT), what a consent form must contain, how to handle the distinction between mandatory and voluntary participation, and how to ensure General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) compliance throughout.
Data collection for an RCT involves collecting personal and firm-level data from participants who have a right to know what that data will be used for, who will have access to it, and what their choices are. Informed consent is the mechanism through which those rights are exercised. Getting it right is a legal requirement under GDPR and a precondition for ethical evaluation practice.
The GDPR is the central legal reference for any collection of personal data in the EU, and its requirements should be consulted carefully when designing the consent form and the wider data-handling arrangements. This page offers practical guidance, not legal advice. The applicable legal bases and national rules depend on the programme and the member state, so involve your Data Protection Officer from the start and consider bringing in legal consultants to review the consent form and any data-sharing agreements.
This page covers what informed consent means in the context of firm-level RCTs under EU Cohesion Policy, what a consent form must contain, how to structure it, and what special considerations apply when evaluation data is collected alongside a programme application.

title: Informed consent in RCT data collection
text: This page explains what informed consent means in the context of a European Union (EU) randomised controlled trial (RCT), what a consent form must contain, how to handle the distinction between mandatory and voluntary participation, and how to ensure General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) compliance throughout.

title: Informed consent in RCT data collection
section: What informed consent means in this context
text:
What informed consent means in this context
Informed consent is a participant’s freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous agreement to the processing of their data for a defined purpose. In the context of an RCT, it covers two distinct activities that must be kept clearly separate:
Programme participation - applying for a grant, entering an eligibility process, and being subject to randomised selection. This is governed by the legal basis for the programme, not by consent. Firms cannot meaningfully consent to or refuse the administrative processing that is required to run the programme.
Evaluation data collection - providing information for research purposes beyond what is required for the programme: extended administrative data tracking, AI-assisted data quality checks, or follow-up interviews. This is where genuine informed consent applies. Firms must be able to choose whether to participate in each optional activity without any consequence for their programme eligibility.

Never bundle consent to evaluation data collection with consent to programme participation. A firm that must tick a consent box to submit its application is not giving free consent - it is being coerced. Under the GDPR, consent is not freely given if participation in a programme is conditional on agreeing to data processing that is not necessary for that programme.

title: Informed consent in RCT data collection
section: What a consent form must contain
text:
What a consent form must contain
A consent form for RCT data collection should cover the following elements.

1. Identity and purpose
State clearly who is conducting the research, who the data controller is, and what the evaluation is designed to find out. Name and provide contact details for:

The Managing Authority (data controller and primary contact)
Any research partners with access to the data (e.g. World Bank, university)
The Data Protection Officer of each data-processing party

The purpose statement should be broad enough to cover the full range of anticipated uses - including future policy reports and academic publications - without being so vague that participants cannot understand what they are agreeing to.

Romania (South-Muntenia)
This survey is being conducted by the […] Regional Development Agency and the World Bank. The goal of the evaluation study is to assess the effectiveness of innovation grants on the creation of successful innovation projects by SMEs and SMEs’ business outcomes and competitiveness.



2. What data will be collected and why
Describe each category of data that will be collected, clearly distinguishing between:

Mandatory data - required for programme administration and collected under a legal basis other than consent
Optional data - collected solely for research purposes and requiring explicit consent

For each optional category, explain what it is, why it is useful to the research, and what happens if the participant declines.


3. The randomisation
Explain clearly that the evaluation uses a randomised design: all eligible firms have an equal chance of being assigned to the treatment group (invited to apply for the grant) or the comparison group (not invited). Participants must understand this before they enter the process. The explanation should be plain and non-technical.

Romania (South-Muntenia)
To achieve a rigorous and unbiased evaluation, the selection of eligible firms invited to submit a formal application is randomised. Information from this form will be used to establish a baseline list of eligible firms. A random sample will then be assigned to the treatment group (invited to fill out the formal application) and the remaining firms will be assigned to the control group (not invited to formally apply).



4. Who will have access to the data
Name every party that will have access to the data, in what capacity, and under what safeguards. If data will be transferred outside the European Union - for example, to the World Bank as an international organisation - state this explicitly and specify the transfer mechanism (Standard Contractual Clauses, adequacy decision, or the organisation’s own data protection framework).


5. How long data will be retained
State the retention period for each category of data. For extended administrative data tracking - such as access to tax and registry records - the retention period specified from the date of submission should be long enough.


6. Confidentiality and anonymisation
Explain how the data will be protected and confirm that no individual firm or person can be identified from published results. Publications, reports, and academic studies must present findings exclusively in aggregate, anonymised, or statistical form.


7. Voluntary participation and the right to withdraw
State explicitly that:

Participation in optional data collection activities is voluntary
Declining or withdrawing consent carries no penalty and does not affect programme eligibility
Withdrawal of consent can be exercised at any time, in writing, and does not affect the lawfulness of processing that already took place
Upon withdrawal, the participant may also request deletion of their data



8. Participant rights under GDPR
Inform participants of their rights: access to stored data (including a free copy), rectification of inaccurate data, data portability, restriction of processing, and the right to lodge a complaint with the national supervisory authority. Provide the contact details of both the Managing Authority’s Data Protection Officer and the relevant national supervisory authority.


9. Duration of participation and follow-up
State how long the initial form will take and whether participants may be contacted for follow-up purposes. Where follow-up surveys or subsequent evaluation rounds are planned, participants should know at baseline that they may be contacted again and for how long this may continue.


10. Signature and confirmation
The form must be signed by an authorised representative of the firm - founder, owner, Chief Executive Officer, or other legal representative. Record the representative’s first name, last name, and obtain a signature (electronic or physical). Confirm that the choices were made freely and without coercion.

title: Informed consent in RCT data collection
section: Structuring the consent: mandatory core and optional modules
text:
Structuring the consent: mandatory core and optional modules
A best practice is to structure the consent document as a short checklist of distinct processing activities, each with its own tick box. This makes the mandatory/optional distinction visible and enforceable, and creates a clear audit trail of what each participant agreed to.
Example:

  
    Box 1 - Randomised programme participation (required)
    Covers participation in the evaluation study, acknowledgement of the randomised selection methodology, data sharing with the World Bank for monitoring and research, and consent to be contacted for follow-up questions for up to six years. This box is required to proceed with the application.
  
  
    Box 2 - Direct institutional access to transactional data (optional - important for evaluation quality)
    Authorises the Managing Authority, acting directly or through the World Bank, to access historical, current, and future firm data from national fiscal and corporate registries - including tax authority, trade registry, and the Ministry of Finance. Valid for up to ten years from form submission.
  
  
    Box 3 - Document quality control via secure AI tools (optional - important for evaluation quality)
    Permits the use of secure AI tools to cross-check the consistency of submitted textual descriptions and financial statements (such as balance sheets). The AI tools do not retain or store data; all information remains under the sole control of the survey provider.
  


Box 1 is required. Boxes 2 and 3 are optional but described as important for the quality of the evaluation. Firms must be able to tick Box 1 without ticking Boxes 2 or 3, and the programme must function correctly regardless of which optional boxes are selected.

title: Informed consent in RCT data collection
text:
Special considerations for EU RCTs
Ethical approval. Research involving human subjects - including firm-level surveys - typically requires ethical approval from an Institutional Review Board (IRB) or equivalent body. Managing Authorities working with a university or international research partner should confirm that ethical approval has been obtained and that the consent form has been reviewed as part of that process.
Data transfers to international organisations. If the research partner is based outside the EU - such as the World Bank - the data transfer must be covered by an appropriate GDPR mechanism. The World Bank processes personal data under its own institutional Privacy Policy, consistent with its mandate as an international organisation established by its member countries. This must be stated in the consent form and in the data-sharing agreement between the Managing Authority and the research partner.
Control group consent. Firms in the comparison group are also research subjects - they are surveyed, tracked in administrative data, and their outcomes are used in the analysis. They must receive the same information notice and consent form as treatment group firms. The only difference is that they are not invited to apply for the grant.
Plain language. The consent form will be read by firm owners and managers, not lawyers. Legal citations are required for completeness but must be accompanied by plain-language explanations.
Multilingual forms. Where the programme operates in a non-English-speaking member state, the consent form should be available in the local language.

Step 5 determined where the data will come from. This step is about how and when to collect it. For most randomised controlled trials (RCT) evaluations of competitiveness programmes, this means planning at least one round of primary survey data collection - a baseline before the intervention - while also coordinating access to the administrative data sources identified in Step 5. Whether a primary endline survey is also needed depends on the availability of administrative data, as described below.

title: Step 6: collect data
text:
Summary
This page covers when and how many data collection rounds to plan, why surveys are used and which method to choose, who to collect from, the role of external data collection firms, how to design and pilot the questionnaire, how to minimise attrition, and General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) compliance requirements.

title: Step 6: collect data
text:
Plan the data collection rounds
An RCT evaluation requires data at multiple points in time. The exact rounds depend on the Theory of Change (ToC) and the data sources available, but the standard structure is:
Baseline survey: conducted before the intervention begins and might be used as the basis for randomisation companies into treatment and comparison groups. It captures pre-treatment characteristics, enables balance checks after randomisation, and provides the benchmark against which post-intervention outcomes are compared. It must be completed before randomisation is revealed. A baseline primary survey is almost always needed, since administrative data rarely contains the intermediate outcomes and mechanism variables required by the evaluation.

North-East Romania: baseline survey
A baseline survey (pre-application data) was administered: the primary objective of the baseline survey was to conduct an initial evaluation of the business’s digital tool requirements and help determine their programme eligibility. The survey questions covered topics such as location, sector, financial considerations (e.g., profits, capital, assets, liabilities), and legal prerequisites. The survey required approximately an hour to complete and was completed online by each firm between June and the end of September 2023.

Follow-up data collection: measures outcomes after the intervention, at a point when effects are realistically expected to have materialised. In the European Union (EU) context, a dedicated endline survey is not always necessary. Business registries, tax records, social security data, and customs records - consistently available across member states - can cover many of the core outcome variables (turnover, employment, exports, productivity) without placing any additional burden on firms. Where administrative data provides sufficient coverage, it should be the primary endline source. A primary endline survey becomes necessary only when the evaluation requires outcomes or mechanisms that administrative records do not contain - for example, management practices, innovation behaviour, digital technology adoption, or respondent-reported perceptions of the programme.

North-East Romania: follow-up data collection
A follow-up survey was administered: the 1,038 firms surveyed at baseline were contacted for a follow-up survey conducted between March and May 2025. Interviews took approximately 60 minutes to complete and covered nine key topics i) general administrative details about the business; ii) background information on the business manager; iii) an overview of the business; iv) details on products/services, market presence, revenue, and customers; v) the use of telecommunications and internet across business locations; vi) relevant digital indicators for the business; vii) methods and processes used for routine business operations; viii) key factors influencing technology adoption, such as investments and management decisions; and ix) financial information for the business in 2024.

Midline survey (optional): where the Theory of Change includes important intermediate outcomes worth tracking before the final endline - for example, changes in management practices or technology adoption as precursors to longer-term productivity effects - a midline round may be warranted. Include a midline only if it is required to answer a specific evaluation question, not as a routine addition.
Administrative data timing: access to administrative records should be requested and negotiated well in advance of the baseline. These sources typically come with a reporting lag of one to two years, which must be factored into the evaluation timeline. The advantage is coverage: administrative data tracks all firms in the sample, including those who do not respond to surveys, making it a more complete picture of outcomes than a survey endline alone.
In the EU, the consistent availability of firm-level administrative data - tax records, business registries, social security data - means that a primary endline survey can often be avoided. Prioritise administrative data for core financial and employment outcomes; reserve primary survey rounds for the outcomes and mechanisms that only firms themselves can report on.

title: Step 6: collect data
text:
Why surveys?
Surveys are the most widely used tool for collecting primary data in impact evaluations of public support programmes. They make it possible to gather structured, comparable information directly from the firms, individuals, or organisations that a programme is designed to benefit - capturing precisely the outcomes and mechanisms that administrative records do not contain.
A particular strength of surveys is their scalability. Rather than collecting information from every single beneficiary or firm in a target population, a well-designed survey can be conducted on a carefully selected subset - a sample - and, provided that sample is representative, the findings can be generalised with confidence to the full population.
For programmes evaluating competitiveness and innovation outcomes - such as changes in firm-level Research and Developemnt (R&D) investment, technology adoption, or management practices - surveys are often the only way to capture the intermediate outcomes that sit between a grant payment and a long-term productivity gain visible in national statistics. They are also essential for understanding why an intervention worked or did not, by measuring the mechanisms that link the programme’s activities to its results.

title: Step 6: collect data
text:
Paper vs. electronic surveys
While paper-based surveys remain in use in some contexts, electronic surveys are the clear standard for programme evaluations today and should be the default choice. Digital surveys offer built-in data validation - mandatory fields, range checks, and logical skip patterns - catching errors at the point of entry rather than during analysis. They eliminate manual transcription entirely, are faster to deploy, easier to monitor in real time, and simpler to adapt if pilot testing reveals problems.

title: Step 6: collect data
text:
Choose a collection method
There is no single best method. The right choice depends on who the respondents are, what the questions require, and the available budget. Three methods are in common use:
Computer-Assisted Telephone Interviewing (CATI) involves trained interviewers conducting structured surveys over the phone. CATI reaches a broad range of respondents quickly and is well-suited when response rates need to be actively managed - interviewers can follow up with non-respondents and clarify questions in real time. It is also practical when beneficiary contact details are already held in programme management systems. Surveys must be kept short enough to hold respondents’ attention on the phone.
Computer-Assisted Personal Interviewing (CAPI) takes the form of face-to-face interviews conducted with a tablet or laptop loaded with survey software. The personal interaction tends to produce more nuanced and accurate answers, particularly on sensitive topics such as firm finances or employment decisions. CAPI is best reserved for complex questionnaires and small, geographically concentrated samples - it is the most expensive method and carries a risk that the interviewer’s presence influences responses.
Web surveys are sent to respondents via email or embedded in an online platform, inviting them to complete the survey at their own pace. They are the least expensive method and can be deployed quickly to large samples, making them well-suited to digitally comfortable populations such as SMEs and technology firms. Response rates for unsolicited web surveys are often low, so active follow-up is essential.
In practice, methods can be combined: begin with a web survey, follow up with CATI for non-respondents, and use CAPI selectively for subgroups where richer detail is needed.

North-East Romania: primary respondents
Data in North-East Romania was collected using a web survey (baseline survey) and involved CAPI and CATI methods for the follow-up survey, depending on respondents’ availability.

title: Step 6: collect data
section: Who to collect from, and when
text:
Who to collect from, and when
Choosing the right respondent. For firm-level surveys, the ideal respondent is a senior decision-maker - a Chief Executive Officers (CEOs), Chief Financial Officer (CFO), or equivalent - who has oversight of the firm’s strategic and financial decisions. The respondent should ideally be the same person at baseline and endline to ensure that differences reflect real changes rather than differences between respondents. Where the programme targets a specific group within the firm - such as R&D personnel - those individuals may be more appropriate for certain questions.

North-East Romania: primary respondents
The primary respondents were CEOs and/or firm owners, with additional input from senior representatives of relevant departments when necessary.

Timing within the calendar. Surveys targeting firm employees are best conducted during standard working hours. August is a poor time to survey firms in most European countries due to summer holidays; the end of the financial year is also problematic, as finance teams are occupied with closing accounts. Be mindful of survey fatigue - beneficiaries who are contacted repeatedly for monitoring and reporting purposes may become less willing to participate over time.

title: Step 6: collect data
section: The role of data collection firms and evaluation consultants
text:
The role of data collection firms and evaluation consultants
Managing Authorities can implement RCTs in-house including conducting surveys and data analysis. However, implementing RCTs comes with many specificities and challenges. The technical expertise needed can be contracted in. Having the right expert team on board makes all the difference. What Managing Authorities need is a well-crafted Terms of Reference (ToRs): the document that attracts the right teams, sets the methodological bar, and defines the conditions for a credible, policy-relevant evaluation. A strong ToR is therefore not a procurement formality - it is the Managing Authority’s most important contribution to the quality of the evaluation. For more information on ToRs, please click here: Terms of Reference
The division of responsibilities between the Managing Authority, the evaluation consultant and/or the data collection firm should be made explicit in procurement. Close collaboration is key for a successfully conducted RCT. Depending on which activities the Managing Authorities conduct in-house, the evaluation consultant or data collection firm supports or conducts the following activities: designing the survey instrument, translating and piloting the questionnaire, determining the sample, setting up the digital survey platform, recruiting and training enumerators, managing fieldwork, monitoring response rates, implementing quality controls, delivering a clean dataset, and carrying out the statistical analysis once data has been collected.

North-East Romania: primary respondents
The survey implementation was undertaken by a team of 30 enumerators hired by Romanian-based data collection firms.

title: Step 6: collect data
text:
Designing the questionnaire

Start with what already exists
Before writing a single question, review existing, validated survey instruments. Using questions that have already been tested in comparable evaluations and surveys saves time, improves data quality, and makes findings comparable with evidence from other programmes and regions. Key reference sources include:

Community Innovation Survey (CIS) - the standard EU framework for measuring innovation activity in firms
Firms Adoption of Technology Survey (FAT) - World Bank instrument on technology adoption across sectors
World Bank Enterprise Surveys (WBES) - firm-level outcomes including investment, productivity, and the business environment
World Management Survey (WMS) - management practices across firms and countries
Flash Eurobarometer on SME Digitalisation - digital technology adoption and skills across EU member states
ECB Survey on Access to Finance of Enterprises (SAFE) - financing conditions and constraints for SMEs


The survey question repository collects questions from the surveys listed above, organised by topic - from company details and financial performance to innovation, digitalisation, and management practices. Use them as a starting point: pick the questions that match your indicators, consult similar evaluations and underlying survey instruments, and adapt the questions to your programme.
Browse the survey question repository



Questionnaire design
A good questionnaire is clear, concise, and purposeful. Every question should map to an indicator in the ToC. Questions included for general interest add respondent burden without adding analytical value and should be removed.
Questions should address only one idea at a time. Double-barrelled questions - which ask about two things simultaneously, such as “Did the grant improve your firm’s R&D capacity and export performance?” - make it impossible for respondents to give an accurate answer and should always be avoided. Wording should be neutral: leading questions undermine the reliability of the data.
Response scales - such as Likert scales or numerical ratings - should be consistent across the questionnaire and clearly labelled. Questions should flow in a logical sequence, moving from general topics to more specific ones. Sensitive questions - such as those about turnover, profitability, or employment figures - are best placed towards the end, once some rapport has been established.
Questions that ask about quantities, values, or periods of time should always specify the unit and reference period explicitly - state the currency (e.g. €), the unit of magnitude (e.g. full-time equivalents, thousands of euros), and the exact time reference (e.g. “in the last financial year, ending [month]”) directly in the question text or as a visible instruction above the response field.
Where surveys are conducted in multiple languages, the questionnaire should be professionally translated and then back-translated to verify that meaning has been preserved accurately.


Piloting the questionnaire
No questionnaire should go into the field without first being tested. A pilot survey - conducted with a small group representative of the target population - reveals problems invisible on paper: ambiguous wording, questions that take too long to answer, response options that do not cover the full range of experiences, and technical glitches in digital forms. The questionnaire should be revised based on pilot findings before full deployment. Skipping the pilot almost always costs more in the long run through lower data quality and analytical workarounds.

title: Step 6: collect data
text:
Minimising attrition
Attrition - firms that cannot be reached or refuse to participate at endline - is one of the most common threats to the validity of an RCT. Even modest attrition becomes a serious problem if it is higher in one group than the other, since differential attrition can bias the impact estimates. Prevention is far easier than correction, and the groundwork must be laid at baseline.
Collect robust contact information at baseline. Record multiple contact points for each firm: the primary respondent’s name, direct phone number, and email; a backup contact; and the firm’s main address and website. Ask respondents explicitly for permission to follow up at endline and to contact them via alternative channels if the primary contact changes.
Maintain a tracking database throughout the intervention period. Do not wait until the endline survey to discover that contact details have gone stale. Update the database periodically using public business registry records, programme monitoring data, and any contact made for compliance or monitoring purposes.
Make re-contact as easy as possible at endline. Send advance notices before the endline fieldwork begins. Use the same survey mode as the baseline where possible, as familiarity reduces refusal rates. Keep the endline survey as short as the evaluation objectives allow - respondent fatigue is a leading cause of non-response in follow-up rounds.
Document and report all non-response. Record the reason for every non-response using standardised codes (firm refused; firm could not be reached; firm closed; firm no longer eligible). This documentation is essential for the attrition analysis in Step 7.

title: Step 6: collect data
text:
Data protection and GDPR compliance
For EU Managing Authorities, compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is a legal obligation that applies to any data collection exercise involving personal data. Before any survey goes into the field, the following must be in place:

A clear legal basis for processing personal data - typically the legitimate interest of the Managing Authority in evaluating public spending, or the explicit consent of respondents
An informed consent process: respondents must be told how their data will be used, how long it will be retained, and who will have access, before they agree to participate. More information on informed consent
Anonymisation or pseudonymisation of responses wherever possible
Appropriate data security measures, including restricted access to identifiable data

Managing Authorities should involve their Data Protection Officer early in the design process - not as a final approval step, but as part of initial planning. Data sharing agreements with third-party survey firms or external evaluators must address GDPR requirements explicitly.

Once the ToC is in place, it becomes the blueprint for selecting indicators. Every element of the ToC - inputs, activities, outputs, short- and medium-term outcomes, goals, and assumptions - needs at least one measurable indicator to track whether things are moving as expected.
For Managing Authorities, some of this work is already done. Some European Union funding programmes (e.g. the European Regional Development Fund) operate within a mandatory performance framework that includes common output and result indicators set by the European Commission. These provide a useful starting point, but they are generally not sufficient for a RCT. Common indicators are designed for monitoring - they tell you what was delivered - but an evaluation also needs to measure what changed as a result, and to do so in a way that allows for comparison with a counterfactual (i.e. what would have happened without the programme).
Indicators for evaluation purposes therefore need to go beyond the mandatory monitoring set and capture the intermediate and final outcomes described in the ToC.

Choosing indicators: where to start
Indicators rarely need to be built from scratch. Managing Authorities should draw on existing, well-tested measures from comparable evaluations before designing new ones. The selection of outcomes and their definitions in this repository was informed by the EuroCOMP Lab evaluations (see Examples), policy reports such as the World Bank’s TIDES report, and established indicator manuals such as the OECD Oslo Manual for innovation and the OECD Frascati Manual for research and development. Drawing on these sources improves the quality of your data and makes findings easier to compare with evidence from other programmes and regions.

title: A legal basis for random selection
text:
This page covers the legal preconditions for using randomisation under EU Cohesion Policy, the key elements any national legal framework must address, and country examples from Spain and France showing how RCTs have been embedded in law.
For a Managing Authority to use randomisation as part of its beneficiary selection process, the legal framework governing that programme must either explicitly permit it or be flexible enough to accommodate it without ambiguity. Most national frameworks were designed around two conventional selection methods - ranking proposals by score, or first-come-first-served - and say nothing about random assignment. A clear legal basis is the precondition for experimental evaluation to happen at all. DG Regio provided formal confirmation that randomisation is permissible under Euorpean Union (EU) Cohesion Policy rules. The key regulatory anchor is Article 44 of the Common Provisions Regulation (EU) 2021/1060, which requires Managing Authorities to evaluate the effectiveness of their programmes but does not prescribe the method - creating space for RCTs as the most rigorous option available.

title: A legal basis for random selection
text: This page covers the legal preconditions for using randomisation under EU Cohesion Policy, the key elements any national legal framework must address, and country examples from Spain and France showing how RCTs have been embedded in law.

title: A legal basis for random selection
section: Key elements any legal framework must address
text:
Key elements any legal framework must address
Regardless of the legislative level - national law, implementing regulation, or programme-specific instrument - the following elements should be covered.

Explicit permission to randomise, with a two-stage process. Randomisation must be framed as applying after eligibility assessment, not instead of it. Stage 1 assesses all applicants against pre-defined competence-based criteria. Stage 2 randomly assigns equally eligible applicants to treatment and control groups. This makes clear that the lottery does not replace merit-based selection - it determines who among equally deserving applicants receives support when the programme is oversubscribed.
Conditions for use. The legal text should specify when randomisation is permissible: there must be a clear research question, measurable outcomes, genuine oversubscription, a sufficient sample size confirmed by a power analysis, a pre-registered evaluation protocol, and informed consent from all applicants at the point of application.
Transparency and documentation. The randomisation algorithm, software, and results must be documented, stored, and publicly communicated. Notarial certification of the draw is recommended. All applicants - selected and non-selected - must be informed of the outcome and the reason for it.
Protection of the control group. Non-selected eligible applicants must retain the right to apply to future calls. Providing equivalent support to control group members through parallel instruments during the evaluation period should be avoided wherever possible, to prevent contamination of the results.
Role of expert panels. Expert evaluation panels assess eligibility in Stage 1. Their role ends once the eligible pool is defined. The randomised algorithm determines selection from that point - panels do not rank or choose among eligible applicants.
Data access and independence. The evaluation must be conducted by an independent team. Data-sharing agreements with administrative data holders (tax authorities, business registries) must be in place before the evaluation begins, with GDPR compliance addressed explicitly.

title: A legal basis for random selection
text:
Country examples

Spain: a royal decree as legal foundation
Spain provides the most developed example of embedding RCTs in a national legal framework for public funding. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the Spanish government established its Inclusion Policy Lab as part of the Minimum Income Scheme and Social Shield policy. The lab ran 32 RCTs with €200 million in funding, partnering with leading academic institutions including Nobel Laureate Abhijit Banerjee and J-PAL Europe. Evaluated interventions - including personalised employment services for the homeless and digital skills training - showed significant improvements in employment rates and life satisfaction. The legal foundation was provided by Royal Decree 378/2022 (Real Decreto 378/2022, de 17 de mayo), which formally integrated RCTs into the use of public funds under Spain’s Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan. The Decree outlined the responsibilities of subsidy recipients participating in pilot evaluations, mandated coordination with beneficiary entities, and promoted evidence-based policymaking, transparency, and accountability as explicit legal objectives.
Two factors were critical to the Spanish success. First, the initiative was framed as a social investment rather than an administrative requirement - this framing secured the political backing needed to pass the legislation and maintain it through a change of government. Second, when the May 2023 elections brought a new administration, a Memorandum of Understanding signed between the World Bank and the regional government of Extremadura prior to the elections ensured continuity in the evaluation process. The MoU covered technical advice on evaluation design, scoring mechanisms, randomisation of applicant selection, and independent outsourcing of the evaluation to prevent political influence.


France: constitutional amendment as enabling legislation
France adopted a higher-level approach, embedding the right to conduct policy experiments directly in the 2003 constitutional amendment, which added provisions under Articles 37-1 and 72 of the French Constitution allowing local and national authorities to run policy experiments. This constitutional foundation enabled 300 policy experiments by 2019, including the Youth Policy Lab (€150 million in public funding, supported by economists Esther Duflo and Marc Gurgand), which led directly to legislative reforms in education and health insurance.

title: Power calculations: how many firms you need
text:
This page explains what a power calculation is, what goes into it, and what a Managing Authority needs to know to have a useful conversation with an evaluator about sample size.
A power calculation sounds technical. In practice it answers one practical question: do you have enough firms to detect whether the programme works? This page explains what drives that number, how to think about it without needing to do the maths yourself, and what to do if the answer turns out to be no.

title: Power calculations: how many firms you need
text: This page explains what a power calculation is, what goes into it, and what a Managing Authority needs to know to have a useful conversation with an evaluator about sample size.

title: Power calculations: how many firms you need
section: The core problem: too few firms and you may miss the truth
text:
The core problem: too few firms and you may miss the truth
Imagine a programme that genuinely improves firm productivity by 8%. If your evaluation includes only thirty firms, the natural variation between those firms - some were already growing fast, some were already struggling - may easily produce an 8% difference between treatment and comparison groups by chance alone. You cannot tell whether the programme caused the difference or whether chance did. The programme may work, but your evaluation cannot prove it.
Add more firms and the picture becomes clearer. With enough observations, the average outcomes in the two groups settle down and genuine differences become visible. The variation that masks the signal shrinks relative to the size of the groups.



Too few firms










Real impacts may go undetected: ordinary differences between firms drown out the programme’s effect.




Enough firms










Real impacts become measurable: averages settle and the difference stands out.




More firms do not make the lottery fairer - they make its answer visible.

title: Power calculations: how many firms you need
section: What drives the required sample size?
text:
What drives the required sample size?
The number of firms you need depends on two things that pull in opposite directions.



The size of the effect you want to detect


A programme that doubles firm turnover is easy to spot even in a small group. A programme that increases turnover by 5% requires a much larger group to detect reliably.
Small expected effect → more firms needed. Large expected effect → fewer firms needed.




How much firms vary from each other


If all firms in the target population are very similar - same size, same sector, similar starting performance - a small sample is enough to pick up a difference. If firms vary enormously, you need more of them to be confident that a difference reflects the programme rather than the mix of firms you happened to include.
High variation → more firms needed. Low variation → fewer firms needed.




Think of trying to hear a quiet voice in a noisy room. A louder voice needs no particular conditions to be heard. A quieter voice needs a quieter room - or more people listening carefully. More firms are the equivalent of reducing the noise.

title: Power calculations: how many firms you need
section: The four ingredients a power calculation combines
text:
The four ingredients a power calculation combines
A power calculation takes four inputs and returns a single number: the minimum sample size the evaluation needs. The evaluator handles the calculation; the Managing Authority needs to understand what the inputs mean so that the conversation about sample size is grounded in the programme’s actual context.


  
  Expected effect
  
  Variation
  (standard deviation)
  
  Confidence level
  
  Statistical power
  
  
  POWER CALCULATION

  Required sample size

  the study needs


Here is what each ingredient means in plain language:
Expected effect. What is the smallest improvement in your primary outcome that would be meaningful enough to be worth detecting? This is a policy judgement, not a statistical one. If a 5% increase in firm R&D spending would be considered a success, that is your expected effect. If only a 25% increase would change how the programme is designed in the next round, use that. Evidence from similar programmes in other regions or member states can help anchor this number. The smaller the effect you want to reliably detect, the more firms you will need.
Variation between firms. How much do firms in your target population differ from each other on the outcome of interest, even before the programme starts? This is usually estimated from existing data - a prior round of the programme, national statistics, or a comparable survey. The evaluator will handle this, but it is worth knowing that the more heterogeneous your target population, the larger the required sample.
Confidence level. How willing are you to risk concluding that the programme worked when it actually did not? The standard is a 5% risk - meaning the evaluation is designed so that a false positive would only arise by chance in 1 out of 20 identical studies. This does not normally need to be changed.
Statistical power. How willing are you to risk missing a real effect? The standard is 80% - meaning the evaluation has an 80% chance of detecting a genuine effect if one exists, and a 20% chance of missing it. For evaluations where a null result would have major consequences - for example, if it would be used to cancel a programme - 90% power is preferable, but requires a larger sample.

North-East Romania: Was 1,038 companies enough for North-East Romania? Once the power calculation is run, you compare the result against the size of your eligible pool. If your pool exceeds the required sample, you are ready to randomise. If it falls short, you need to grow the pool before the draw.
In North-East Romania, the evaluation team ran the power calculation before the draw and confirmed that the pool of 1,038 firms was large enough to detect the effects they expected - which is why the draw proceeded with 519 firms in each group.

title: Power calculations: how many firms you need
section: Always randomise more firms than you need at endline
text:
Always randomise more firms than you need at endline
The power calculation tells you how many firms you need to observe at the end of the evaluation - at the endline survey. But not every firm randomised at baseline will still be reachable by then. Some will have closed, relocated, or simply stopped responding. This is called attrition, and it is one of the most common threats to the validity of an RCT.
The practical implication is straightforward: always recruit more firms into the randomised pool than the power calculation requires, to leave a buffer for expected drop-out. If you need 400 firms at endline and expect that roughly one in five will be unreachable by then, you need to randomise at least 500 firms at baseline.
The evaluation team will advise on the right buffer based on comparable studies, the expected follow-up period, and the availability of administrative data - which, in the EU, can often be used to track firms that drop out of surveys.

Attrition is not just a power problem. If firms drop out at different rates in the treatment and comparison groups - for example, if struggling firms in the comparison group are more likely to close - the two groups stop being comparable and the impact estimate becomes biased. Step 7 covers how to detect and address this.

title: Power calculations: how many firms you need
section: What if there are not enough firms?
text:
What if there are not enough firms?
If the power calculation reveals that your eligible pool is too small, there are six practical fixes. The right combination depends on what is driving the shortfall.

  
    Increase outreach
    More applicants mean a larger eligible pool. North-East Romania ran outreach events in more than 20 cities before the application window opened, specifically to ensure the pool would be large enough.
  
  
    Expand eligibility
    Lowering the eligibility threshold adds more firms to the pool. Be careful not to expand so broadly that the evaluation no longer answers the original question - the expanded population should still be the one the programme is designed to serve.
  
  
    Combine regions or cohorts
    If a single region or programme round does not produce enough firms, pooling two regions running similar programmes - or two consecutive cohorts - into a single evaluation can reach the required sample without changing the design.
  
  
    Run a phase-in
    Rather than running the programme to all eligible firms at once, stagger rollout across waves. Each wave that is still waiting acts as the comparison group for the waves already receiving support - doubling the effective sample without needing more firms overall.
  
  
    Focus on where effects are largest
    If the expected effect is larger among a specific subgroup - younger firms, firms in a particular sector, firms with no prior R&D experience - narrowing the focus raises the detectable effect and reduces the required sample. This only makes sense if the narrowed population remains policy-relevant.
  
  
    Invest in a strong baseline
    Collecting good baseline data on the primary outcome - before the intervention - and using it in the analysis significantly reduces the sample size needed. The evaluator can explain how much this helps in your specific context; the reduction is often substantial.

title: Power calculations: how many firms you need
section: A practical note for Managing Authorities
text:
A practical note for Managing Authorities
The power calculation is usually the evaluator’s job - not the Managing Authority’s. But the Managing Authority is the only party that can answer the policy question that drives the most important input: what effect would be large enough to matter?
A Managing Authority that can say “we would consider the programme successful if it increased firm R&D spending by at least 15%” gives the evaluator something concrete to work with. A Managing Authority that leaves that question open will get a power calculation based on assumptions it may not recognise or agree with - and may end up with a required sample that is either impossibly large or so small that meaningful effects cannot be detected.

The conversation about sample size is one of the most important early conversations between the Managing Authority and the evaluation team. Have it before the programme design is finalised - not after the eligible pool is already fixed.

title: Step 2: define learning questions
text:
Summary
This page covers why learning questions must come first, what makes a good learning question, the four types - primary, heterogeneity, mechanism, and implementation - how to link them to the Theory of Change (ToC).

title: Step 2: define learning questions
text:
Why evaluation questions come first
The ToC developed in Step 1 sets out the causal logic of the programme. Evaluation questions translate that logic into a concrete analytical agenda: they specify which links in the causal chain will be tested, which outcomes will be measured, and what the evaluation can credibly claim to have shown at the end.
Getting this step right matters more than it might appear. Vague or poorly scoped evaluation questions lead to data collection that is too broad, analysis that is unfocused, and findings that cannot be clearly attributed to the programme. Conversely, well-formulated questions make every subsequent decision easier - they tell you which indicators to select (Step 3), which data sources to prioritise (Step 5), and what the evaluation team will need to deliver.

title: Step 2: define learning questions
section: What makes a good learning question?
text:
What makes a good learning question?
A well-formulated learning question has four characteristics:
Specific. It names the intervention, the target population, the outcome of interest, and the time horizon. Generic questions such as “did the programme work?” are not answerable. A specific question might be: does receiving an R&D grant increase a firm’s total R&D expenditure within two years of the award?
Causal. For an RCT, the central question is always about causation - not correlation. The question should be framed in terms of the effect of the programme, not merely whether outcomes changed. This means the question implicitly requires a comparison: between supported firms and comparable firms that did not receive support.
Answerable. The question must be answerable with the data and methods available. An evaluation that asks about 10-year productivity effects but only has a two-year window will not be able to answer its own primary question. Scope questions to what the evaluation can credibly deliver.
Decided in advance. Evaluation questions must be set before data collection begins - not after. Questions formulated after seeing the data are prone to selective reporting and undermine the credibility of the findings. Pre-registration on a public registry (see Step 3) locks in the questions publicly before any results are observed.

title: Step 2: define learning questions
text:
Types of learning questions
A well-structured evaluation typically includes a primary question and a set of secondary questions. These serve different purposes and should be clearly distinguished.
The primary question focuses on the main effect of the intervention on the most important outcome. This is the question the evaluation is powered to answer - the sample size and data collection plan are designed around it. For most competitiveness and innovation programmes, the primary question concerns a key outcome such as R&D expenditure, product innovation, or labour productivity.

North-East Romania: primary question
Does receiving a digitalisation grant increases business performance (e.g. sales) and productivity?

Heterogeneity questions ask whether effects differ across subgroups - for example, by firm size, age, sector, or prior innovation experience. These questions are important for understanding for whom the programme works best and informing targeting decisions in future programme rounds.

North-East Romania: heterogeneity question
How do impacts of receiving a digitalisation grant vary across firm size, location, sector, and initial level of digitalisation?

Mechanism questions probe how the intervention produces its effects - which links in the ToC are activated. By measuring intermediate outcomes, these questions open the “black box” and generate richer policy lessons than a simple estimate of the final effect.

North-East Romania: mechanism question
Does the digitalisation grant increase investments in digitalisation and technology adoption?

Implementation questions assess whether the programme was delivered as intended and what barriers affected take-up or compliance. These are particularly important for interpreting null results - an evaluation that finds no effect needs to establish whether the intervention was actually delivered.

North-East Romania: implementation question
What share of companies in the treatment group, that were invited to apply, were actually contracted?

title: Step 2: define learning questions
section: Linking learning questions to the ToC
text:
Linking learning questions to the ToC
Every learning question should map to a specific link in the ToC. A useful discipline is to write out the ToC and, for each arrow connecting two levels, ask: do we have a question that tests this link? If a link is left untested, either the evaluation is under-powered to examine it, or the link is assumed to hold without evidence.

title: Step 2: define learning questions
text:
Scoping and realism
Evaluation questions must be scoped to what the evaluation can credibly deliver. Two common pitfalls are worth flagging:
Over-ambition. An evaluation that promises to answer questions about long-term productivity effects, regional spillovers, and mechanisms simultaneously may not be powered to answer any of them well. Prioritise the primary question and be selective about secondary questions.
Attribution. Learning questions should be scoped to what can be attributed to the programme, not to broader trends. If a question asks whether firms in the region became more innovative, the answer will reflect macroeconomic conditions and parallel policies as much as the programme itself. A well-scoped causal question asks about the difference between treated and comparison firms, not about levels.

text:
This page covers the internal team to assemble before starting and seven sequential steps - Theory of Change (ToC), learning questions, indicators, feasibility, data sources, data collection, and data quality - for designing a credible randomised controlled trial (RCT).
A well-designed RCT does not begin with randomisation - it begins with a clear understanding of what the programme is trying to achieve and why. The seven steps below set out the preparatory work that makes randomisation meaningful and the results credible. Managing Authorities are encouraged to work through them in sequence, ideally before the first call for applications is launched.

title: How to design a randomised controlled trial
text: This page covers the internal team to assemble before starting and seven sequential steps - Theory of Change (ToC), learning questions, indicators, feasibility, data sources, data collection, and data quality - for designing a credible randomised controlled trial (RCT).

title: How to design a randomised controlled trial
section: 7 steps for designing an RCT successfully
text:
7 steps for designing an RCT successfully


Step 1: develop a preliminary Theory of Change
Map the causal logic of your intervention - from inputs to long-term goals - and make the assumptions explicit.


Step 2: define learning questions
Formulate the specific questions the evaluation is designed to answer, grounded in the ToC.


Step 3: determine relevant indicators
Select the outcome indicators that will be used to measure change across each level of the ToC.


Step 4: check whether an RCT is feasible
Check whether the conditions for a valid RCT are in place - oversubscription, timing, legal basis, and political buy-in.


Step 5: identify available data sources
Decide whether to rely on primary data, administrative data, or a combination - and map what is already available.


Step 6: collect data
Design and implement the data collection - surveys, administrative data access, and quality controls.


Step 7: ensure high-quality data
Put in place the checks needed to detect and address data quality problems before analysis begins.

title: How to design a randomised controlled trial
section: Before you start: assemble your internal evaluation team
text:
Before you start: assemble your internal evaluation team
The Managing Authority brings knowledge that no outside expert can replicate - how the programme works in practice, who the target firms are, what the political constraints are, and what a meaningful result would look like. External consultants and data collection firms are available to provide methodological and operational support, and many Managing Authorities will choose to work with them. But whether the RCT is implemented with external support or largely in-house, a core internal team needs to be in place from the start. Without it, key decisions get made by default rather than by design, and the evaluation risks being shaped by what is convenient rather than what matters.
Before working through the seven steps, identify who inside the Managing Authority will take on each of the following roles:

An evaluation focal point - the person who leads the process, coordinates across the other roles, and serves as the primary contact for the external evaluation team. Ideally someone with some familiarity with impact evaluation methods, or who has been through the EuroCOMP Lab training.
A programme manager - someone with detailed knowledge of the intervention: eligibility criteria, selection process, implementation timeline, and the population of applicants. This is the person who can answer the policy questions that drive the evaluation design - particularly what effect size would be meaningful and what the programme is realistically expected to achieve.

Where possible, it is also helpful to involve a legal or procurement officer early - to confirm that the national legal framework permits randomisation and to manage the procurement process - and a data protection officer, to ensure that data-sharing agreements and General Data Protection Regulation compliance are in place before fieldwork begins.
The internal team does not need to be large - in smaller Managing Authorities, one or two people may cover several roles. What matters is that the responsibilities are clearly assigned and that the evaluation focal point has the authority to make decisions and the access to programme information they need.
Where internal capacity or methodological expertise is limited, external experts can be hired to support - covering evaluation design, data collection, or both.

section: Monitoring and evaluation (M&E) vs impact evaluation
text:
Monitoring and evaluation (M&E) vs impact evaluation



M&E


Collect data on inputs, outputs, outcomes and participants to

Improve day-to-day management and decisions
Make descriptive before and after comparisons



Describes what is happening, but not whether it is because of the intervention.




Impact evaluation


Collect data on participants and comparison groups to

Find the causal impact of a programme
Find the most effective way to deliver a programme
Support cost-benefit analysis



Determines impact in a way that can only be attributed to the programme, by establishing what would have happened without it.



Monitoring and impact evaluation are complements, not alternatives. An impact evaluation should not go ahead without solid monitoring data: who applied, who was selected, who was contracted, and what they invested in. Without that, you cannot tell whether a programme had no effect or was simply never implemented as planned.

title: Why and when to use a randomised controlled trial
section: What exactly is the impact of a programme?
text:
What exactly is the impact of a programme?
Definition. Impact is what happens after a programme is introduced, minus what would have happened in its absence, the counterfactual.
The dilemma. The counterfactual is a “what if” and is unknown to us. Ideally, we would observe the same applicant twice, once with the programme and once without it, and compare. That is impossible: each applicant either takes part or does not. Every impact evaluation method is a way of approximating that missing second observation.
The solution. Find a way to construct the counterfactual so impact can be measured. This can be done in different ways. The page shows different methods of constructing the counterfactual and explains why RCTs are considered the gold standard.

Note: Impact is the causal effect of the programme: the gap between what happened with it and what would have happened in its absence.


Impact is measured using outcomes
When evaluating projects, often only outputs are assessed, because they are the easiest thing to count. Measuring impact means moving from counting outputs to measuring outcomes.


Outputs
What a programme delivers. For example, grants disbursed, firms enrolled, training sessions run.


Outcomes
What changes because of it. For example, growth, jobs, innovation, resilience.



The impact in the North‑East Romania programme
For North-East Romania, the impact is the gap between treatment and comparison firms on four tracked outcomes: digital adoption, revenue, employment, and productivity.

Before implementation, map out how a programme’s activities are expected to change the problem you are addressing. That shows, in advance, why each step should lead to the next. That causal logic, the how and why behind each step, explains a programme’s reason for existing. It also tells you what you need to measure in order to test whether the expected change is actually happening.

  Inputs

  Outcomes

But which outcomes should one look at exactly? A programme can change many things, and not all of them can or should be measured. To know which outcomes to look at, and when to expect them to change, start by spelling out how the programme is supposed to work: how its inputs and activities lead to outputs, and how those outputs are expected to lead to outcomes.
This chain is the foundation of a theory of change, and having thought it through helps in designing a strong impact evaluation. There is more on this in Step 1: develop a Theory of Change.
Making the chain explicit also surfaces the assumptions behind each link, and shows which of them the programme’s impact depends on most. If one of these assumptions does not hold (for example, that firms will take up the support they are offered), the programme may fall short of its intended impact. One way to reduce this risk is to test, within the same evaluation, alternative ways of addressing that weak link, such as two different outreach approaches, and see which works better.

Digitrans example The Digitrans pilot (see Examples for more details) tested and compared two alternative ways to increase digital adoption among MSMEs in Bulgaria, Poland and Slovakia. Firms were randomly assigned to either (i) a comparison group receiving no support, (ii) a financial subsidy alone, or (iii) the same subsidy paired with technical assistance.
The pilot found that money alone was not the most effective approach. Firms that also received technical assistance used digital tools 2.5 times more intensively than those with the subsidy alone. This is evidence that capability, not just cash, was a constraint to digitalisation.

title: Why and when to use a randomised controlled trial
section: What does good allocation of public resources look like?
text:
What does good allocation of public resources look like?
Return on public investment is the benefit attributable to a programme divided by its cost. “Attributable” requires knowing what the programme beneficiaries would have done in the absence of the programme (the counterfactual).
That is especially hard when beneficiaries are not assigned to programmes at random but are selected by the Managing Authority. Beneficiaries may differ from those that were not selected, e.g. they may be more motivated or have more resources. Most of these traits are never recorded in any database or questionnaire. When the beneficiaries later do better on the outcomes of interest than the applicants that were not selected, it is impossible to tell how much of that difference is due to the programme.
Consider an illustrative innovation-grant scheme: EUR 50,000 to each of 100 firms, where “success” means launching a new product. Compare two selection rules.



Strategy A: fund the top performers


Firms that succeed: 80 of 100
Would have succeeded anyway: 65
Succeeded because of the grant: 15
Additionality rate: 19%


Strategy A looks stronger at the first glance as it is associated with 80 successes but only 15 of these succeeded because of the grant.




Strategy B: fund the marginal firm


Firms that succeed: 55 of 100
Would have succeeded anyway: 20
Succeeded because of the grant: 35
Additionality rate: 64%


Strategy B causes 35 successes and thus is more impactful than A.



Raw success counts can be misleading. Programmes need to be judged on impact, not on raw success to evaluate their effectiveness.


Deadweight: low additionality
Additionality is the share of activity that would not have happened without the programme. Top performers would likely have invested anyway, so public funds mostly substitute for money they would have spent regardless - generating little that is truly additional per euro.


Selection bias in measurement
Comparing funded, stronger firms with unfunded, weaker ones credits the programme with firms’ pre-existing quality, not with what the grant did.


Where the grant buys most
Support actually changes behaviour for the marginal, constrained firm: the good project that could not otherwise get funded.


Can experts spot the marginal firm?
Evidence suggests not reliably. In a business plan competition in Nigeria, judges’ scores did not predict which firms would survive or grow three years later (McKenzie & Sansone, 2019; see Common myths).

title: Why and when to use a randomised controlled trial
text:
Finding the counterfactual
As defined above, the counterfactual is what would have happened to programme participants without the programme. It can never be observed directly, so it has to be estimated.
Strategy. Find a group of firms that on average look like treated firms would have looked in the absence of the programme. This group is the comparison group.
There are two ways of estimating the counterfactual:



Ex-ante: Randomised controlled trials


Create the comparison group up front, by randomly assigning who receives the programme. Randomisation is what guarantees the two groups look the same on average.




Ex-post: quasi-experimental designs


Look for a suitable comparison group after the programme has already been rolled out, using natural variation in who received the programme and who did not.




Selection bias is the risk that the comparison group does not actually look like the treatment group on average. If that assumption is wrong, the impact estimate is biased.


North‑East Romania: the counterfactual In North-East Romania, the counterfactual is the group of eligible firms that were not drawn in the lottery. How the lottery created it.

What is a randomised controlled trial?
Intuition. Randomly assign the programme so one group receives it (the treatment group) and one does not (the comparison group). Because the two groups start out the same, the comparison group’s outcome shows what would have happened to the treatment group without the programme.

Note: Treatment and comparison groups start at the same outcome level and diverge after the programme, with the divergence being the impact of a programme.

Because assignment is decided by chance, the two groups are alike on average not only in characteristics you can measure, but also in those you cannot. Take the example of firms applying for a grant: randomising who receives the money means that, on average, the two groups look the same on observable characteristics such as size, sector or turnover, and also on unobservable ones such as management quality or motivation. Nothing should systematically differ between them except that some applicants were lucky in the draw and others were not. That is why no statistical adjustment for firm characteristics is needed to get a credible estimate.

What “random” means here. Not randomly sampling a sub-population to study, but randomly deciding, among qualifying applicants, who receives the programme and who does not.

Advantage. RCTs are considered the gold standard of quantitative impact evaluation because:

No assumptions about outcome levels or trends between groups are necessary, as long as randomisation is implemented correctly
They deliver strong evidence
They are easy to interpret

section: Randomisation can improve legitimacy and trust in programmes
text:
Randomisation can improve legitimacy and trust in programmes
Randomly selecting beneficiaries among eligible applicants is fair. When more applications are eligible than there is budget to fund, a lottery is a transparent way to decide who gets in. It treats every eligible applicant the same rather than relying on favouritism or timing.
Illustration:

North‑East Romania: additional measures to increase trust
North-East Romania’s draw was run in front of a notary: the random number seed drawn, the selection code run, and the resulting balance between groups reviewed. This increased firms’ confidence that selection was fair. The draw also made selection faster. Because beneficiaries were drawn at random from the eligible pool, no ranking of the “best” applications was needed. Evaluators only had to check that each firm met the formal criteria and that the requested funds were justified.

section: What do you want to learn?
text:
What do you want to learn?
Whether you have sufficient evidence that your programme works, or you are still working out who it reaches and how to design it, there is a case for experimentation. The starting question is whether the programme is working as well as it could be.



Does the programme cause an effect at all?


You do not yet know whether the programme works, or you are still working out who it reaches and how it should be designed before it starts. This requires finding a credible comparison group before the programme launches. Example: in North-East Romania, a lottery decided which eligible firms were invited to apply for a digitalisation grant, and the others formed the comparison group (see above).




How do you deliver it better?


You already know the programme works. The programme’s implementation may already be ongoing. What you want to know is which version of the programme works best. Example: The Digitrans example compares whether a grant alone versus a grant combined with technical assistance performs best.




North‑East Romania: testing outreach In fact, the North-East Romania programme asked both questions. It used an experiment to find out if the programme is effective and a second experiment to study how to best conduct outreach. Before the digitalisation call, the regional development agency randomly selected 26 of 46 towns for in-person information visits, in which a consultant explained the call and helped firms complete the pre-assessment survey. The visited towns produced 110 applications against 71 in the towns that did not receive in-person visits (55% more). The additional applicants in towns with in-person visits were smaller firms (12.6 employees on average, compared with 19.6).


Colombia: group vs individual management support Iacovone et al. 2022 compared two ways to deliver management consulting to auto-parts firms: one-to-one (about US$28,950 per firm) and in groups of 3-8 firms (about US$10,500). Both raised management scores by around 9 percentage points, but only group consulting significantly raised sales and profits.
